Inspect Steward is a system for automated execution and supervision of long-running evaluations. Steward enables you to launch a large run and walk away while a coding agent monitors it and automatically intervenes when required. 

- Evaluation runs are fully unattended by design, but can escalate to humans when required.

- Opinionated defaults for error handling keep tasks running, with an agent driven workflow for error resolution and retry.

- Slack notifications to keep operators apprised of status and pending decisions.

- Works with a standard [Eval Set](https://inspect.aisi.org.uk/eval-sets.html), as well as with runners like [Inspect Flow](https://meridianlabs-ai.github.io/inspect_flow/) and [Inspect Hawk](https://hawk.metr.org).
::::













## Introduction

Inspect Steward runs an eval set the way a person would if they sat in front of it all night — and then does the sitting for you.

A steward acts on behalf of someone who isn't there. That is the relationship this package models: you start a run and step away, and the steward minds it. Concretely, Steward:

1.  Enumerates what a definition resolves to **before** anything runs, so you can see what you are committing to.
2.  Runs each task in its own process, so one crash costs one task rather than the run.
3.  Reconciles the log directory against that enumeration on a schedule — spawning what should be running, recording what died, and leaving alone what is already done.
4.  Reports where the run stands cheaply enough to ask constantly.
5.  Says what needs a person, once each, rather than every ten minutes.

You do not have to be there for any of it, and neither does a coding agent. A timer guarantees the mechanical half; the parts that need judgement wait for someone who can exercise it.

### If you already use `eval_set()`

Steward is not a replacement for `eval_set()` — it *calls* it. Your definition stays exactly what it is today: a program culminating in one `eval_set()` call. What changes is who orchestrates.

|  |  |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **One process per task** | `eval_set()` runs an eval set in one process, so an OOM or a segfault takes the whole run with it, and every task's Python work — transcript construction, JSON serialization, `.eval` compression, non-model scorers — serializes behind the GIL on one core. Steward spawns one worker per task, so a crash is isolated and CPU-bound work actually runs in parallel. |
| **Load you chose rather than load that emerged** | Inside one process, sample concurrency adapts to what the provider allows. Across N processes, N independent controllers each discover headroom the others have not claimed yet, overshoot together, and get throttled together. Steward owns both factors — how many workers, and each one's share — so the fleet's demand is a number you set. |
| **Errored samples become a work list** | Steward runs workers with `fail_on_error=False`, so a task always reaches the end of its dataset. That means a log can say `success` while carrying errored samples, and **completion is not success**. What you get instead of a silent pass is an explicit queue of samples that need a decision. |
| **A record of how the run was conducted** | Which samples were re-run, which were accepted as failed, who decided, and why — kept as it happens rather than reconstructed afterwards. |

Everything downstream still works, unmodified and live: one flat log directory means `inspect view`, `samples_df()`, and `inspect log` see exactly what they would see if you had run `eval_set()` by hand.

## The shape

``` text
       your definition                        one flat log directory
   (evalset.py / flow.yaml / hawk.yaml)
              │                                   task₁.eval
              │  read once                        task₂.eval
              ▼                                   task₃.eval
          manifest  ────────────┐                      ▲
     (every resolved task)      │                      │
                                ▼                      │
                          steward tend  ───► worker ───┘
                       (reconcile, spawn,   one task,
                        reap, record)       one process
                                ▲
                                │  every ~10 minutes
                            the timer
```

Steward reads your definition once to learn what it resolves to — the **manifest**. From then on, a **tend** compares that against the log directory and closes the gap: anything wanted with no log gets a worker, anything finished is left alone, anything the definition no longer asks for is moved aside. Miss a tend and nothing breaks; the workers already running keep running, and the next tend picks up where the last one left off.

## Who does what

Supervising a run is not one job, and Steward's central design decision is where it draws the lines. Four parties, in order of how much judgement each exercises:

| party | does | exercises judgement? |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **the timer** | makes a turn happen on a schedule | no |
| **`steward tend`** | reconcile, spawn, reap, archive, record, write the snapshot | no — and it never does long work, so it always returns in seconds |
| **a coding agent** | tunes concurrency, groups error classes into questions you can answer, investigates, writes up what happened | yes |
| **you** | decide what is being measured, rule on anomalies, answer approvals, sign off | yes, and some of it is yours alone |

The reason to care about the split is that **each party's absence fails differently**, and only some of those failures are acceptable overnight:

| what is missing | what happens |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| nothing | the fleet converges, questions get answered as they arise, the run ends in an attestation |
| **the agent** | the fleet still converges — logs land, the snapshot stays current, nothing stalls. What accumulates is judgement: unruled anomalies, untuned concurrency, nothing written up. A run waiting for a decision, which is a fine thing to be at 4am. |
| **the agent and you** | the same, for longer |
| **the timer** | nothing happens at all, *and nothing says so* — silence is indistinguishable from a healthy run. This is the failure the whole arrangement exists to prevent, which is why `launch` arms a timer or refuses. |

There is one exception worth knowing about before you rely on the second row. A worker that stops on a tool approval or an `ask_user` is alive, holding its slot, and waiting for a *person* — not the timer, and not the agent, which is barred from answering. A definition with human approvers therefore loses throughput as well as accumulating decisions. Steward reports those loudly, but it cannot resolve them.

### Moving work down the stack

The table above is not fixed. `_steward.md` in your workspace is how you hand work to a party that needs less judgement than you do:

- Writing `max_workers: 8` in its front matter turns a judgement into a constraint Steward enforces unattended, with nobody in session.
- Writing *"re-run samples that failed on provider rate limits, up to twice, without asking"* in its prose turns a decision you would otherwise be woken for into one the agent may act on, because you already made it.

Rules accumulate as you notice yourself answering the same question twice, and the run gets quieter as they do. See [Standing Rules](directives.qmd).

## Getting started

``` bash
pip install inspect-steward
```

Steward runs on macOS and Linux. Windows is not supported: a run has to outlive the process that started it, and the detached-process, control-socket, and process-table mechanisms that achieve that are POSIX-only.

Then create a workspace:

``` bash
steward init my-sweep
```

That is a directory a person and an agent co-inhabit, and that a third party can pick up cold — everything important is written down rather than held in somebody's session. See [The Workspace](workspace.qmd) for what each file is for.

## Running a sweep

### 1. Write the definition

A definition is **any program culminating in a single `eval_set()` call**. `init` leaves an empty placeholder; what goes in it is exactly what you would write anyway:

``` {.python filename="evalset.py"}
from inspect_ai import eval_set

from my_evals import mbpp, gsm8k

eval_set(
    tasks=[mbpp(), gsm8k()],
    model=["openai/gpt-5", "anthropic/claude-opus-5"],
    log_dir="logs",
    max_samples=40,          # <1>
    retry_on_error=3,        # <2>
)
```

1.  Set this explicitly. It is the difference between sample concurrency Steward can retune on a live worker and concurrency it can only watch.
2.  How many attempts a flaky sample deserves is a property of your eval, so it stays yours. It is also the *only* automatic recovery tier — past it, every further attempt is a decision.

An Inspect Flow spec and a Hawk eval set config are definitions too, and Steward drives their own entrypoints rather than reimplementing them. See [Definitions](definitions.qmd).

### 2. See what it resolves to

``` bash
steward tasks
```

This executes the definition to enumerate it and prints one row per resolved task — task × model × solver, with sample counts. Nothing runs. This is the moment to notice that a sweep is four times larger than you meant it to be.

### 3. Launch

``` bash
steward launch
```

`launch` reads the definition, commits the manifest as desired state, spawns the first workers, arms a timer, and **returns**. It does not block, because the thing that supervises the run is not the terminal you typed into.

Check what it armed:

``` bash
steward timer status
```

### 4. Walk away

From here the run tends itself. Each turn spawns what should be running, reaps what died, rewrites `status.md`, and appends what it observed to the journal.

### 5. Come back

``` bash
steward status
```

`status` is `tend` with its actions discarded — the same reads, the same decision, nothing carried out. So it reports both where the run stands *and* what the next turn would do, and it is safe to run as often as you like:

``` text
⚠️ 1 needs a person
4 tasks: 2 complete, 1 incomplete, 1 missing

task            samples  done  running  queued   score
mbpp@gpt-5      500/500  100%                    0.742
mbpp@opus-5     500/500  100%                    0.781
gsm8k@gpt-5     318/500   64%       38     144   0.669
gsm8k@opus-5      0/500    0%

3 running · next tend: 1 to spawn

## attention

### needs a person

- gsm8k@opus-5 has stopped making progress after 3 attempts and will not be
  respawned — `stalled:gsm8k@opus-5:3`
```

For what each part means, see [Reading Status](status.qmd).

If you need to change the sweep — add a model, raise epochs, fix a task argument — edit the definition and run `steward launch` again. A workspace is a project rather than a single run, and amending it is the same verb as starting it. See [Amending a Run](amending.qmd).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### Not yet implemented

The arc above ends at `status`. The half that turns an attention list into settled results — anomalies with a lifecycle, notification that reaches you when you are not at a terminal, and `steward signoff` as an attestation that you accept the results — is designed but not yet built. Until it is, a run's open questions are answered by a person reading `status` and deciding, and a run has no terminal state beyond "nothing is progressing".
:::

## Responsible use

Steward exists to start long, expensive work and stop watching it, and both halves of that deserve respect.

- **Know what you are committing to.** `steward tasks` enumerates the whole sweep before a dollar is spent. A definition that crosses four models with three epochs over two thousand samples is twenty-four thousand samples, and that is visible in advance rather than discovered in the morning.
- **Steward does not manage spend.** It does not track, project, cap, or act on cost. The real control is upstream of the run: run less. Per-sample limits belong in your definition, and account-level budgets belong to your platform.
- **A `success` log is not a good result.** Because sample errors never fail a task, a task whose model API was down for its entire duration completes "successfully" with a meaningless score. Read the attention list, not the exit code.
